summary: Foundation Aviation Under Fire Over Charter Disputes and Litigation
details:
Foundation Aviation and Firm Foundation Aviation have recently faced growing scrutiny within the private aviation industry due to multiple breach-of-contract lawsuits, collection actions, and customer complaints alleging unpaid obligations, canceled trips, and disputed charter funds. Public court filings show several companies and aviation vendors pursuing legal action against the firms throughout 2025 and 2026.
One of the most widely discussed cases was filed by ATI Jet, Inc. d/b/a JetVia in federal court in Texas. According to the complaint, JetVia alleged that Foundation Aviation accepted approximately $80,000 for a charter flight, later canceled the trip, and failed to promptly return the funds. The lawsuit further alleged a pattern of financial instability, operational disruptions, and repeated disputes with counterparties. It is important to note that these are allegations made in litigation, and the claims have not necessarily been proven in court.
Additional public records show other businesses filing commercial disputes against Firm Foundation Aviation, including claims involving collections, breach of contract, and unpaid balances. Cases referenced in public filings include actions by Hillsboro Aviation, Austin Business Finance, Thoro Corp, and other aviation-related entities.
Within industry circles, concerns have also circulated regarding alleged last-minute aircraft substitutions, delayed refunds, and charter scheduling issues. Some aviation forums and charter industry discussions have characterized the company’s practices as aggressive or unreliable, though many of those discussions consist of opinions and unverified claims rather than adjudicated facts.
As with any aviation provider, customers and brokers are generally advised to conduct due diligence before entering into charter agreements. That can include reviewing DOT and FAA operating authority, verifying aircraft control and insurance documentation, and examining publicly available litigation history and financial disclosures where applicable.

summary: Moser Aviation Draws Industry Attention Over Regulatory Issues”
details:
Moser Aviation has faced significant FAA enforcement scrutiny in recent years, drawing attention throughout the Part 135 charter industry over alleged regulatory and operational violations. While the company has continued operating, public records and FAA filings have raised concerns regarding management oversight and compliance practices.
In July 2022, the FAA proposed a civil penalty of more than $3 million against Moser Aviation, alleging the company conducted 1,018 charter flights without a qualified chief pilot in place between January 2020 and May 2021. According to the FAA, the operator allegedly failed to notify regulators within the required timeframe after the chief pilot position became vacant and continued operating revenue flights during that period.
The FAA further alleged that Moser Aviation falsely informed the Denver Flight Standards District Office that its previous chief pilot was still serving in the role after the position had reportedly become vacant. Those allegations became the basis for one of the larger proposed civil penalties issued against a Part 135 operator in recent years. It is important to note that FAA enforcement actions are allegations unless fully adjudicated or settled.
Beyond the FAA enforcement action, discussions within aviation forums and pilot communities have included allegations involving maintenance concerns, operational pressure, and aggressive management practices during periods of rapid expansion. Some former employees posting publicly online described concerns about aircraft dispatch reliability and operational decision-making, although many of these statements remain anecdotal and unverified.
Public aviation violation databases also show prior FAA safety-related penalties associated with Moser Aviation before the larger 2022 enforcement matter, suggesting regulators had previously taken action involving compliance issues tied to the operator.
As with any charter provider, brokers, passengers, and aircraft owners are generally encouraged to independently review FAA records, operator certificates, insurance documentation, and publicly available enforcement history before conducting business with a Part 135 operator.
